comments.author: Trobador
comments.text:
As much as I like Tildes and understand the premise that we should all be trying to consider each others' opinions, I'm saddened by how people on here seem to not only accept genAI programming so readily, but also completely dismiss ethics when justifying why they do so.

There's a few people on here implying this would only be relevant if it only excluded vibe-coded projects, not AI assistance. That only the resulting product matters. Did we forget everything we were criticizing large models for in the first place?  Do we just not care that the tool itself is based on stolen work? That continued use and support of it is actively destroying the environment for little benefit? That its growing commodity is causing a general decrease in individual knowledge and learning capacity? That it's making the industry of IT that most of the people commenting belong to worse to be a part of? Like, surely, a bit more than just the result matters here?

Ethics matter. Call it a purity contest or virtue signaling or whatever, I don't care. Trying to do something good to push against the bullshit even if it's imperfect and still has to rely on tech that does use it to exist and be effective is still better than doing nothing at all. This is a good thing and I have no criticism to make of it.

comments.author: kacey
comments.text:
Yo 👋 I'm personally trying to tone down how much confrontation I cause in this space, but I wanted to minimally note my disapproval. Framing this as a black and white ethical issue equally saddens me, since that same absence of nuance and appeal to morality has been used to justify atrocious actions throughout history. And it erases any good that the tools can accomplish. Furthermore, given the amount of personal attacks I get whenever I mention LLMs/AI here, I sincerely doubt that there's a majority of people who agree with me -- you are almost certainly in the majority. I'd imagine people who hate this have artificial intelligence filtered out of their tags, or otherwise avoid the topics.

(edit: sigh ... I had hoped this wouldn't be exemplary'd. For anyone reading this, fwiw, the person was pleased with the notion of trying to keep conversations calmer. It wasn't an AI thing)

comments.author: JCAPER
comments.text:
Framing this as a black and white ethical issue equally saddens me


I was going to give an exemplary label because of this, but I wanted to show publicly why I 100% agree with your point.

I'm so, so, so tired of this 0 or 1 attitude. You're either 100% in favour of something, or 100% against it. It feels like nowadays on the internet you can't stand somewhere between both. This attitude I feel is more destructive in the long run.

I, for example, think:


Image and Video Gen AIs overall are more bad than good, because of the impact they have on real artists and the dangerous potential for misinformation (which I feel it's only going to get worse as these models get better)

Still, from a purely technical stand point, I'm blown away by these things. Think about it: we "taught" sand to make videos! How cool is that!?

These models were and are being trained without consent, and people are rightly pissed off about it. I'm not an artist but I want to make video games, I would also be pissed off as well if someone used my games without consent

But these models are a genie that are out of the bottle now. Are we supposed to pretend they don't exist? Should the americans 70 years ago pretended jet engines weren't a thing because the Nazis invented them? I don't think so.

I'm fatigued as well about almost every company wanting to shove AI into every single piece of software. It's nuts, it's stupid, I'm against it. It's a privacy nightmare as well and the wet dream for Google and others.

LLM's allowed me to finally make my own homelab and troubleshoot some niche things on Linux. I'm building something I always wanted to have at home, and I'm learning new skills as I go along.

On the other hand, I do feel the "temptation" of offloading thinking process to the model. I've been disciplined to always thinking of the solutions myself and let the LLM execute, but I imagine many people are not doing the same (be it in coding context or others). I worry if/when these companies decide to influence the public opinion, if they aren't already.


I have a lot more thoughts, but these zigzag of thoughts should be good enough to illustrate my point. No one will ever convince me that these things are the best thing ever - we shouldn't underestimate some of the societal dangers these could potentially have. But neither will no one ever convince me that my own experiences are wrong, and that LLMs didn't have some good outcomes for my own skills and work.

comments.author: Zorind
comments.text:
I haven't posted on here a lot about LLM stuff, but I keep reading most of it...or at least, most of the threads on it, which have not been great for me mentally.

I think I'm fairly anti-ai, but I have a hard time really examining my position because I know how emotionally biased I am in it.

I am not an artist. I have never been very "creative", but I love the thought of being creative.

I loved legos growing up, and I think most of that is because it let me put things together

in ways that were creative and showing creativity, but did not require me to be "good" at it.

I was never able to get into drawing or anything like that in the same way, and I've always

loved reading comics and seeing what artistic people are able to create.

I went to school for programming, because I truly love writing code & seeing things happen as a result.

To me, programming has been my "creative" output.  So I find myself biased against LLMs generating code, for what I imagine are the same emotional reasons as a lot of artists, but not necessarily the reasons that get sympathy or could actually have legal repercussions (e.g. training on stolen art).

But also I struggle with it myself, becuase like, am I gatekeeping?  Am I against it because it was my "special thing" that many others couldn't do?  I don't think so, but maybe there's some of that to it as well, as to why I don't like it.  But like, at the same time, I'm glad to hear that it has helped you be able to set up a homelab and troubleshoot stuff on Linux.

I think it is great that people are now able to customize software and make tools and stuff that are useful to them, that they would never have been able to "before LLMs". Except, if I look at this from the art angle, I'm not sure how consistent my view is here?

I've never really been good at putting my feelings into words, and I certainly haven't gotten any better at it.  It just seems like most of what I have been good at, are things that now people are using LLMs for.

and I don't know where that leaves me.

I'm going to keep avoiding LLMs for the things I enjoy doing, which is...most of the things I do,

and it does frustrate me seeing LLMs continually invade those things, and it is sometimes saddening

when I see others using LLMs for the things I enjoy doing. I don't think others should necessarily

not use them for those things, because if they don't enjoy doing them, sure, automate it away.

But like, it is much, much too late to put the genie back into the bottle, so all I can really do is personally protest by avoiding using them where I can. And I don't know whether I'm doing that for ethical or emotional reasons, but I'm also not really sure it matters.

I do really appreciate your take here, as well as from @kacey.  I like being able to have some of these nuanced conversations around LLM uses, (or at least, read other peoples nuanced takes when I don't feel like commenting).

comments.author: papasquat
comments.text:
Yeah, I think I'm pretty aligned with you on my feelings around this stuff. I don't mind when other people use AI to help them do personal projects, or when people use it at work to help with work, as long as the quality is still good (big qualifier, I know).

I do absolutely HATE when people diminish the work of other people by commenting that AI could do that, or that it wasn't actually that hard because they did the same thing with AI. It fills me with blinding rage, and it's very common amongst obnoxiously pro ai spaces.

When someone hand builds a complicated piece of software, shares it with the world, talks about the years they've spent on it, and someone comments that AI could do the same thing, I just want to slap them.

Even if it was the same quality, which is extremely dubious, imagine someone going up to a master blacksmith that created a hand forged masterpiece of a sword over months and going "I could get the same thing on temu for 10 dollars".

This unfortunately happens (very common in custom furniture especially), but I absolutely detest the idea.

Even if the results were the same (they basically never are). Someone hand crafted by a human being is special, and will always be more valuable than something mass produced and shitted out by a machine. Even if blacksmithing and furniture making is no longer a viable career in most places, the people those things create has way more intrinsic value to most people, and the same is true for software in my opinion.

comments.author: kacey
comments.text:
I was going to give an exemplary label because of this [...]


Thank you very much for not doing that 😅 I feel that it needlessly escalates tensions on a topic that needs to be discussed (as noted in your comment!).

For my part, I've been wishing for years that the temperature would come down far enough to talk about effective resistance against all this -- job loss via automation, devaluing of the arts, legislative reform, etc. But that requires acknowledging that the problem exists, and dispassionately analyzing the space for asymmetries to be exploited in favour of the common people.

We need to be organizing workers, pressuring local governments, and pushing our vision of what a future with these tools should look like -- not de-facto rolling over and allowing OpenAI/Anthropic/Microsoft/Google to decide for us. Endlessly debating about data centres and morality cannot un-create the idea of a transformer, or delete every open weight model on the internet, but I firmly believe that the window of opportunity remains open for deciding whether the world on the other side of all this is a good one. For whatever definition we -- not Sam Altman or Dario Amodei -- decide "good" is.

comments.author: Lia
comments.text:
Thanks for explaining.

I agree that there isn't much difference in our opinions. I'm just getting tired of seeing people parrot the "AI is here to stay, there's nothing we can do about it" black-and-white doomerism because in most cases it seems to imply that we have to take everything an AI company says or does as unavoidable. Use it or get left behind is another similar soundbite. And so on and so on.

The pain I feel can't be escaped because AI and the toxic people it enables (not you!) are everywhere. It's like a subtle form of torture and I can feel myself developing an allergy-like reaction to it. For example, nowadays just seeing the words "An honest question" feels extremely off-putting. comments.author: kacey
comments.text:
Yeah, that's definitely understandable, and I can relate. I personally find it very distasteful how these massive corporations are shaping the messaging.

Re. my friends, it's a complex situation, but thank you. For what it's worth, I despise the way this whole situation has gone down in ways I lack the words to describe.

The last few months before departing what was to be the end of my software development career, I interrogated myself daily, inwardly considering "does this differentiate me from an AI? And if not, I should automate it away". Writing or reviewing code -- sure. Authoring architectural plans -- alright. Speaking to, or coordinating with teams. OK. Writing peer reviews, reading through applicants' resumes ...

What was the point of it all if there were trillions of dollars being spent on obsoleting me anyways. Why stay on the ride if it clearly ends in a brick wall.

I wanted to be a musician, at one point. I sold that dream for money. I wanted to write fiction, and inspire others to dream. I burned that desire to keep my heart warm in a career that sought to drown me. Friends and family were kept at arm's length, as the only thing I consistently felt was a dull anger. In the end, all I had left was the pride in my work, and I was instructed to sacrifice that too, on the altar of efficiency, to earn my manager a pat on the head (and a coin in their pocket).

I get that none of this is similar to what others are feeling, since if nothing else, experience has taught me that I think and feel in ways that're completely alien to the overwhelming majority of people. But, to relate to others' perspectives, I think back to how I felt when I reached inside to throw one more piece of my soul overboard to stay afloat, and grasped a clenched fist.

Anyways, I'm probably being overly dramatic (and I've had time to reflect and heal anyhow). Point is, I get that peoples' responses are coming from a place of hurt, and I try to give them as much space as possible until they feel comfortable again. It sucks a bit for me, but only insofar as I need to find other spaces to discuss AI topics (as noted elsewhere, the world is not lacking in those) and I need to add another conversation filter to the stack (it's already a mile high, so it's nbd).

comments.author: teaearlgraycold
comments.text:
Do we just not care that the tool itself is based on stolen work?


No I never cared about that. Specifically in the case of code generation I think it's not such a clear cut case. The models are trained on freely distributed copylefted code. Does that mean the resulting AI generated code should be copylefted as well? Maybe. I don't really care if a judge decides AI generated code is all AGPL now. I'd actually be ecstatic if I could make legally enforceable requests to every SaaS company around the world to hand over their now poisoned source code. I'm more than happy to have contributed my public code on GitHub to the model's training data. I've gotten more out than I put in. For image and video generation (which aren't tools I use anyway) there's a much stronger argument against it as so much more of the training data wasn't meant to be freely distributed and copied.


That continued use and support of it is actively destroying the environment for little benefit?


Fair point. And it's a shame because it's mainly an issue of electricity sourcing. It doesn't need to have its current carbon footprint. We should be running 100% renewable electrical grids by now. We are at least making good progress as a species on that. Solar is incredibly cheap, battery tech is improving. I personally wouldn't mind if datacenter expansions were limited by whether they could run off of clean energy.


That its growing commodity is causing a general decrease in individual knowledge and learning capacity?


Depends on the person. I'm able to do new things and learn in the process using these tools. I just finished a project which I will write up and share on Tildes soon. I used LLMs heavily throughout the process (for CAD, programming, data science). I could have done everything by myself, but it would have taken more hours to do so. It's not a kind of project I'd ever done before and I'm quite proud of it.


That it's making the industry of IT that most of the people commenting belong to worse to be a part of?


I'm outside of the software employment world at the moment. Thanks to LLMs I'm hoping to get into a niche area of automated manufacturing soon. I'm highly confident I can build my own CNC machine (not a CNC mill to be clear) given the availability of the basic components/modules/plans online combined with my knowledge and LLMs to fill in the gaps. It helps I have both an industrial warehouse and a makerspace to help me. One aspect I hope to see a tremendous uplift in is patching CNC firmware with LLMs to implement my customizations. Something that could have been a couple weeks of learning will probably be accomplished in a couple of hours. Sure I won't have a personal deep knowledge of the firmware - but I don't think I'll need to. When you build a more standard CNC device you usually don't need to know how the firmware works.

Edit: Honestly if you're someone with technical skills right now I think stretching your capabilities through LLM assistance is a goldmine. Things where you'd typically need to work on a small team (or just be skilled in many areas) can now be accomplished for nearly free as a solo entrepreneur. The LLMs from the top labs are currently subsidized. They only recently got good enough to use in this way. Now's the time to act!

comments.author: post_below
comments.text:
I'm saddened by how people on here seem to not only accept genAI programming so readily, but also completely dismiss ethics when justifying why they do so.


Sorry if I'm being presumptuous but I think what you might mean here is that the denouncing of LLMs isn't as unanimous as you'd like. I'd say there's a pretty even mix of sentiment about AI on Tildes, with hate edging out non-hate.

The second part of the quote is frustrating. It's  blanket assigning a binary sentiment to a large group of people. All anyone can do with that is disagree or ignore it, it's too generalized to be true.

It's far more nuanced. For example, I think AI tools are incredibly useful for some things. Game changing. And I hate that a world changing technology is ultra-capitalized from the start. With the internet we had decades of exploration before the worst of the enshittification set in. That's unlikely to be the case with AI.

And the evironmental concerns are real (if often overexaggerated) and I care about that deeply, I think most people do. I also dislike the potential for AI to contribute to wealth inequality and consolidated control. However, like the internet, AI also increases individual capability. One person, or small groups of people, can accomplish much more than they could before. Sometimes more effectively than big organizations.

Here's the thing: It's not going to go away. It doesn't matter what you think, or I think. If we could somehow burn down all the big AI labs, people would advance the tech in their garages. A new round of funding would launch countless startups in the space. That's because the tech is genuinely useful. There was a lot of emotionally motivated writing about how LLMs don't really help anyone, and anyone who thinks they do is just deluding themselves, in 2024 and even early 2025 but that's painfully outdated. It's only people with no expertise in any of the fields where AI has value that are saying that kind of thing now.

I have nothing against a website listing AI free options. I think it's great, bring on the demand for artisanal, entirely hand crafted, options.

But also the reality is that, in the field of software engineering at large, AI assisted (as opposed to wholly vibecoded) development is already the rule rather than the exception and nothing is going to change that.

comments.text:

That "when" assumes a particular answer to a very big "if". I'm seeing no indication yet that LLMs will ever be used to solve bugs faster than they are used to produce them. The economic incentives are pointing elsewhere: access to models that can thoroughly audit and produce high quality threat analyses that identify critical vulnerabilities is much more expensive than access to models that can produce poor to mediocre code which ostensibly implements solutions to business domain problems but has an error rate similar to that of a junior developer.

There are a few differences between the LLM and the junior developer that further exacerbate the problem. The junior (without an LLM) is limited in their productive capacity by their lack of skill, knowledge and wisdom. They will produce code at a lower rate than the experienced developer, because they will have to stop to learn things more often, ask more questions or will simply avoid problems that seem challenging. The burden imposed on more skilled team members in reviewing and auditing the low-quality code is consequently limited. The LLM knows no such limits and will spit out massive changes without ever gaining knowledge. I think people working in engineering organizations that are being pushy about LLMs can corroborate my experience that this eventually results in lower quality reviews.

I worked in an organization where management "addressed" the problem by reminding developers that their code is their responsibility, whether they wrote or generated. That sounds nice in theory, but is ultimately simply not true. The resulting problems won't magically be directed at the person who created them, but at the team that maintains the software.

You should consider that what works for Linus Torvalds might not work for every other software project. Linux has generally high standards of inclusion because it deals with the production and maintenance of software responsibly and uncompromisingly as a high-stakes engineering problem. Being as widely deployed as Linux is also attracts a lot of attention from security researchers and skilled developers, funded by organizations with legitimate interests in its quality. I am however using (and I'm being used in) a lot more software produced by organizations with much lower standards, driven by the market to "get shit done", "move fast and break things" or whatever other slogans they use to justify being quick to market at the cost of quality of engineering. This use of these systems is often not voluntary.

Meanwhile, with the advent of LLMs, the difference in cost between producing such low quality systems and producing high quality systems has increased. I think it will increase further as investors become impatient waiting for the chatbot vendors to realize the potential they see in them as profitable businesses. If any charlatan with no knowledge of engineering can use an LLM to quickly generate volumes' worth of low-quality software alone and something with the rigor of Linux still demands the attention of hundreds of engineers on the LKML, the production of software will be much more in the hands of incompetent charlatans than people like the Linux maintainers.

comments.author: skybrian
comments.text:
It’s a bit ironic to complain about “copyright laundering” when free software got it start by reimplementing proprietary software. Stallman wrote copylefted code that reimplemented proprietary Unix commands that did the same thing. This was done specifically to evade the licensing requirements of the original software!

And to be clear, I think implementing free alternatives to proprietary software is a good thing, though the software vendor might not like how it undermines their business model. If you’re trying to make a living writing software, competition from free alternatives is a problem. (Free only after they’re implemented of course. Actually building the software still costs time and money, though less than before.)

Sometimes people hoped that free software would become “viral” due to network effects along with copyleft restrictions. But to the extent that it has, it’s mostly not due to the copyright restrictions. Every popular programming language has a huge collection of open source libraries available and copyleft doesn’t play much of a role in that. And now that AI-driven rewrites are feasible, it’s even more dead. It’s too easy to make clones that are free of whatever copyright restrictions you might add.

The remaining “moat” is basically trust, along with inertia. Just because some unknown author published an AI rewrite and it seems to work, would you trust it? How exactly do new projects become trusted? We often depend on network effects - if an open source library has been around for a while and seems to be used a lot, maybe it’s okay? We don’t even know the names of most of the developers whose work we depend on.

When a new version is published under the same name, hopefully upgrading is safe? Nowadays package managers are adding “cooldown” periods so that ordinary developers don’t upgrade immediately. There are organizations that automatically scan new releases for malware, and adding a delay gives them time to sound the alarm. I wonder to what extent these vendors are starting to use AI for their scans?

AI assisted:
